A Salmonella outbreak in Sweden has been linked to a type of produce.

Sixteen people fell sick in the Salmonella Napoli outbreak that was suspected to have been caused by arugula from Italy.

The Public Health Agency of Sweden (Folkhälsomyndigheten) said patients are eight men and eight women. They range in age from less than 1 to 84 and the median age is 57 years old.

Illness onset dates are between Aug. 17 and Sept. 6. There are a couple of cases with later onsets that were either secondary cases or did not have gastrointestinal symptoms.

Twelve ill people were interviewed or replied to trawling questionnaires and eleven of them had purchased arugula from the same supermarket chain. The other person also bought a salad mix containing arugula from this supermarket. All purchases were made within a relatively short period.

One patient kept an empty bag from their purchase of arugula, intending to put it in the plastic recycling. Based on this information, the Swedish Food Agency (Livsmedelsverket) conducted a trace-back investigation.

Traceability of the empty package from one of the cases homes led to Italy. However, this batch of arugula was not sampled since there was no product left.

Salmonella Napoli is not a very common serotype in Sweden with only eight reported cases in 2025.

## Subscribe to Food Safety News

Get the free version of our newsletter. No spam ever, unsubscribe anytime.

After the "Summer of Recalls," many consumers are understandably nervous about food safety, wondering if the industry is doing enough to protect them. Headlines claiming that recalls are up 400 percent this year fueled consumer fear, and the public is now looking for reassurance about the safety of our food supply.

It’s a given that public health must be the highest priority for the food industry. It’s also important to understand the reality we live in today, where the viral nature of information causes claims to spread quickly and widely, without much regard to their accuracy or context. The 400 percent statistic wasn’t necessarily incorrect, but understanding the specific numbers it was representing will help offset consumer fear — without detracting from the responsibility the food industry has to keep consumers safe.

So let me clarify what the number is measuring, what that means for how you shop, and what you can expect from the industry so you can respond to a recall correctly.

A social media creator claimed she had read “something” that said recalls were up 400 percent, but didn’t point to where the number had come from or what it was specifically representing.
